mean: one of the things that causes or shapes a result
ex: Cheap mobile data was a big factor in the rise of short-video apps in small-town India.
ex2: Price was the deciding factor when the Joshis chose a second-hand Alto over a new car.
note: Say 'a factor in' something: 'Price was a factor in my decision.' The verb 'factor in' means include in your plan: 'factor in traffic'.

mean: caused by; because of
ex: The delay in the Rajdhani Express was due to thick fog near Kanpur.
ex2: The India-Australia match in Bengaluru was called off due to rain.
note: Formally, 'due to' follows a noun or 'be' (The delay was due to fog); after a verb, use 'because of' (We left because of fog).

mean: to cause something to happen later
ex: Skipping meals during exam week can lead to headaches and poor sleep.
ex2: A small leak in the roof can lead to damp walls by the end of the monsoon.
note: The past tense is 'led to', not 'lead to': 'The rumour led to a fight.' A very common spelling mistake.

mean: to cause a particular result
ex: One careless forward on the society WhatsApp group can result in a week of arguments.
ex2: Driving on the wrong side of the highway can result in a heavy fine and a suspended licence.
note: 'Result in' goes from cause to effect; 'result from' goes from effect back to cause. Rain results in floods; floods result from rain.

mean: to stop something from happening
ex: Washing hands with soap can prevent many stomach infections during the monsoon.
ex2: A good helmet can prevent serious head injuries in a scooter accident.
note: Say 'prevent him from going', not 'prevent him to go'. Noun: prevention, as in 'prevention is better than cure'.

mean: a result of an action, often a bad one
ex: As a consequence of the transport strike, Kolkata's buses and trams stood still all day.
ex2: Missing the scholarship deadline had one painful consequence: Divya had to take a loan for college.
note: Usually for bad results: 'face the consequences'. 'Of no consequence' means unimportant. 'Consequently' is a connector meaning 'so'.

mean: to make something start suddenly
ex: Dust from the construction site can trigger an asthma attack in Zoya's grandfather.
ex2: One careless remark about the Indian team can trigger a shouting match at a Kolkata adda.
note: Also a noun: 'Dust is a trigger for asthma.' The slang 'triggered' (meaning upset) is informal; avoid it in serious writing.

mean: to be one of the causes of something; also, to give money or help
ex: Late-night scrolling and endless cups of chai contribute to poor sleep among hostel students.
ex2: Rising numbers of cars and two-wheelers contribute to the haze that hangs over Patna every winter.
note: Stress the second syllable: kun-TRIB-yoot, not KON-tri-byoot. It works for bad things too: smoking contributes to heart disease.

mean: a strong effect that something has on someone or something
ex: The new metro line had a huge impact on rents in Thane.
ex2: The coach's half-time talk had a clear impact on how the team played in the second half.
note: As a verb ('This will impact sales'), it is common in offices but informal; in careful writing, 'affect' is better.

mean: the power to change how someone thinks or acts
ex: Her grandmother's stories had a deep influence on Fatima's decision to study history.
ex2: Bollywood songs have a strong influence on how young people in small towns dress for weddings.
note: Stress the first syllable: IN-floo-uns. As a verb, no 'on': 'Ads influence children', not 'influence on children'.

mean: to come from or be caused by something
ex: Most fights in joint families stem from small misunderstandings, not big betrayals.
ex2: Many of the city's traffic jams stem from poor road planning, not just from too many cars.
note: It points back to the cause: 'His anger stems from insecurity.' Past: 'stemmed from'.

mean: an extra, unplanned effect, often bad, especially of a medicine
ex: The doctor warned that drowsiness is a common side effect of the cough syrup.
ex2: One happy side effect of working from home was that Arjun finally got to know his neighbours.
note: Not only medicines: rules and apps have side effects too. Usually written as two words; 'side-effect' is also seen.

mean: to say that something was caused or done by someone or something
ex: Coach Sandhu likes to attribute every win to the 5 a.m. practice sessions in Mohali.
ex2: Shabnam's grandmother likes to attribute her long life to daily walks and no sugar in her tea.
note: Verb stress: uh-TRIB-yoot. The noun, meaning a quality ('Patience is a good attribute'), is AT-rih-byoot.

mean: something that makes a change happen, or happen faster
ex: A viral video of the broken bridge became the catalyst for repairs the village had wanted for ten years.
ex2: Winning the 1983 World Cup was a catalyst for cricket's huge popularity across India.
note: From chemistry: a substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up. Usually 'a catalyst for' something.

mean: real but hidden beneath what you can see
ex: The fever came down, but the doctor at AIIMS wanted to find the underlying cause.
ex2: The underlying reason for the brothers' quarrel was an old dispute over the family land.
note: An 'underlying condition' is an existing illness, like diabetes, that makes a new illness more dangerous.

mean: to have the opposite result from what you planned
ex: Banning phones at home can backfire if teenagers simply start hiding them.
ex2: The shop's plan to raise prices during Diwali may backfire if customers simply order online.
note: Stronger than 'fail': the plan hurts the person who made it. Comes from the bang of a car engine misfiring.

mean: one event causing other effects that keep spreading outward
ex: A failed monsoon has a ripple effect: farmers earn less, tractor sales fall, and village shops suffer.
ex2: When the IT company shut its Pune office, the ripple effect hit nearby canteens, PGs and auto drivers.
note: Picture a stone dropped in a pond. A 'domino effect' is narrower: one thing knocks over the next, in a line.

mean: to stop someone from doing something by making them afraid or unsure
ex: The new CCTV cameras in the lane are meant to deter chain-snatchers.
ex2: The steep fine is meant to deter people from spitting paan on the station walls.
note: Prevent stops something by any means; deter works through fear or doubt. Noun: deterrent. Past tense doubles the r: deterred.

mean: to make a bad situation even worse
ex: Heavy rain will only compound the misery of commuters already stuck on the Western Express Highway.
ex2: Skipping physiotherapy will only compound the problem with Vikram's injured knee.
note: Verb stress: kum-POWND. The noun KOM-pownd is a walled area (the school compound) or a chemical mix.

mean: to make a bad event happen suddenly or sooner than expected
ex: A sharp diesel price hike threatened to precipitate a truckers' strike across Tamil Nadu.
ex2: The captain's sudden injury could precipitate a crisis in the batting order just before the final.
note: In chemistry, a precipitate is a solid that forms in a liquid. 'Precipitation' in weather reports means rain or snow.

mean: to make a problem, pain or bad feeling worse
ex: Burning crop stubble can exacerbate the smog that already chokes Delhi every November.
ex2: Shouting at a crying toddler will only exacerbate the tantrum, the paediatrician told the new parents.
note: Don't mix it up with 'exasperate', which means annoy greatly. Problems get exacerbated; people get exasperated.

mean: to end in an important event after a long build-up
ex: The ten days of Ganeshotsav culminate in the immersion processions on Anant Chaturdashi.
ex2: Months of rehearsals will culminate in the school's annual day show at the town hall.
note: Usually 'culminate in' + the final event. Use it for a high point after a long process, not for any ending.

mean: a bad effect that follows an action, often later and unexpected
ex: One repercussion of the bank fraud was that every customer in the town had to redo their KYC.
ex2: The biggest repercussion of the leaked exam paper was a retest for two lakh students.
note: Mostly used in the plural: 'face repercussions'. More formal than 'consequences', and it suggests effects that spread and last.

mean: showing that one thing directly causes another
ex: A Chennai survey found that filter-coffee drinkers lived longer, but it could not prove a causal link.
ex2: Doctors have long established a causal link between smoking and lung cancer.
note: Not 'casual'! Swapping two letters changes everything. Two things moving together (correlation) does not prove a causal link.

mean: the idea that a tiny event can lead to huge results later
ex: Missing the 7:42 local led to a chance meeting, then a job, then a marriage: the butterfly effect, Mumbai style.
ex2: Gautam calls it the butterfly effect: one extra coaching class led to a new friend, a startup and a move to Bengaluru.
note: From chaos theory: a butterfly's wings could, in theory, help set off a far-away storm. Unlike a ripple effect, the outcome is unpredictable.

mean: a series of things happening quickly, each one causing the next
ex: One tripped power line set off a cascade of failures that left half of North India in darkness.
ex2: The collapse of one big wholesaler set off a cascade of unpaid bills among the small traders of Surat.
note: Literally a small waterfall. In offices, the verb 'cascade the message' means pass it down from bosses to teams.

mean: to change something or someone in some way
ex: Heavy fog in January can affect flights at Delhi airport for hours.
ex2: Too much screen time before bed can affect how well a child sleeps.
note: Affect is usually the verb; effect is usually the noun. 'The rain affected the match; the effect was a draw.'

mean: the final result of an action or event
ex: The outcome of the panchayat election was announced late at night in the school hall.
ex2: Whatever the outcome of the surgery, Dr Menon promised to call the family straight away.
note: Outcome is the end result; output is what a machine or worker produces. Don't mix them up.

mean: because of; usually said about a good cause
ex: Thanks to the new bridge, children from the island village no longer cross the river by boat.
ex2: Thanks to one leaking pipe, the whole building in Andheri had no water for two days.
note: Usually for good causes; used for a bad one it sounds ironic. 'Due to' is more neutral and formal.

mean: to make something start suddenly, like a fire from a small flame
ex: The umpire's decision was enough to spark a heated debate at every chai stall in town.
ex2: A school trip to the planetarium can spark a lifelong love of science in a child.
note: Used for reactions: debates, protests, interest, ideas. 'Trigger' is close but more often for something bad.

mean: to cause a strong reaction, especially anger
ex: Don't provoke the stray dogs near the hostel gate; just walk past calmly.
ex2: The film has an open ending that is meant to provoke discussion, and it did, at every Kolkata adda.
note: You do something, someone reacts. 'Thought-provoking' means something makes you think hard.

mean: to make a feeling or situation stronger or bigger
ex: Rumours on social media can fuel panic buying, as people rush to stock up on salt.
ex2: Every defeat seemed to fuel Lalita's determination to train harder in the boxing ring.
note: Like pouring petrol on a fire: it makes something that already exists grow bigger.

mean: the time after a bad event, and the effects it leaves behind
ex: In the aftermath of the Chennai floods, neighbours shared food, water and phone chargers for days.
ex2: In the aftermath of the final defeat, the dressing room stayed silent for an hour.
note: Used after bad events: floods, wars, defeats. Don't use it for a wedding or a party.

mean: the deepest, main reason a problem happens
ex: Engineers found that the root cause of the daily power cuts was one old, overloaded transformer.
ex2: Good teachers look for the root cause when a bright student suddenly stops doing homework.
note: Fix the root cause, not just the symptoms. 'Root cause analysis' is a common phrase in offices and factories.

mean: something extra that comes out of making or doing something else
ex: Molasses is a by-product of the sugar mills in western Uttar Pradesh.
ex2: Better English was a happy by-product of Farhan's habit of reading the newspaper every morning.
note: Also spelt 'byproduct'. A by-product is unplanned but often useful; a side effect is usually unwanted.

mean: to help something grow or develop over time
ex: Weekly reading circles foster a love of books among children at the village library.
ex2: Good managers foster trust by admitting their own mistakes in team meetings.
note: It also means caring for a child who is not your own: a foster parent. Both meanings are about care and growth.

mean: to make something slower or harder to do
ex: Potholes and waterlogging hinder rescue teams trying to reach flooded parts of Guwahati.
ex2: Constant phone notifications hinder Tanvi's concentration when she studies for the CAT.
note: Hinder slows something down; prevent stops it completely. Say HIN-dur, not HYN-dur.

mean: a possible result of an action, often complicated or unexpected
ex: One ramification of the new data law is that small shops must now keep customer phone numbers safe.
ex2: The biggest ramification of the bank merger was that two thousand staff were moved to new cities.
note: Mostly plural: 'the ramifications of a decision'. Like branches from a tree, one choice spreads into many results.

mean: to encourage something to happen faster or more
ex: Lower interest rates could spur demand for new flats in Hyderabad.
ex2: Her brother's success in the civil services exam helped spur Pooja to start preparing seriously.
note: A spur is a push that speeds things up. 'On the spur of the moment' means suddenly, without planning.

mean: to start something on purpose, often trouble
ex: The police are trying to find out who helped instigate the fight between the two college groups.
ex2: After the food-poisoning case, the hostel committee decided to instigate a full inspection of the mess kitchen.
note: Usually negative: you instigate a fight or a riot. In formal use, a committee can also instigate an inquiry.

mean: a bad situation where each problem causes another that makes the first worse
ex: Poor sleep makes Arnav anxious, and anxiety keeps him awake: a vicious circle he cannot break.
ex2: Many small farmers are stuck in a vicious circle of borrowing to repay old loans before the next crop.
note: 'Vicious cycle' is also common. The happy opposite is a 'virtuous circle', where good results feed each other.

mean: a belief that comes true because people act as if it is true
ex: Telling Kabir he was bad at maths became a self-fulfilling prophecy: he stopped trying and failed.
ex2: When rumours said the small bank would fail, everyone rushed to withdraw money: a self-fulfilling prophecy.
note: Common in talk about exams, markets and parenting: expecting failure can cause it.
